```{r setup}
library(CausalState)
library(SuperLearner)
```

## Overview

`CausalState` estimates the causal effect of a longitudinal **modified
treatment policy** (MTP) on an outcome in care-episode data where patients
can transition out of an active state (e.g. ICU discharge or death). The
distinctive feature is that the MTP can shift the transition dynamics
themselves — not only the terminal outcome. The MTP framework is due to
Díaz & van der Laan (2012) and Haneuse & Rotnitzky (2013).

Two main estimators are provided, both from Luedtke et al. (2017/2018) and
both **sequentially doubly robust (SDR)**: consistent whenever, at each time
point $t$, either the treatment model $g_t$ or the outcome model $Q_t$ is
correctly specified ($2^K$-robust, Definition 2 of Luedtke et al.):

- **`sdr()`** — Sequential Doubly Robust estimator. Applies an EIF-based
  pseudo-outcome update within the backward Q-regression (Díaz et al. 2021).
- **`itmle()`** — Infinite-dimensional TMLE (iTMLE), Algorithm 4 of Luedtke
  et al. Shares the same backward Q-regression as SDR; differs only in the
  update step, which uses an infinite-dimensional TMLE fluctuation.

**`qreg()`** is a pure Q-recursion plug-in (no update step, no DR guarantees)
included as a sensitivity check when density-ratio weights are extreme.

The workflow is always:

```
fit_g()  →  sdr() / itmle() / qreg()
```

`fit_g()` must be run first; all downstream estimators inherit its
fold structure and weights.

---

## Data structure

Data must be in **long format**: one row per subject per time point, covering
only periods while the subject is in the active state. The last row for each
subject carries their transition outcome.

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|--------|------|---------|
| `id` | integer / character | Subject identifier |
| `time` | integer 1, 2, … | Time index |
| `alive` | 0 / 1 | 1 = alive at end of period |
| `in_state` | 0 / 1 | 1 = still in active state (e.g. ICU) |
| treatment | numeric or factor | Numeric binary/continuous; factor categorical; ordered factor ordinal (`a_names`) |
| outcome | numeric | Outcome variable (`y`) |
| covariates | numeric | Baseline and time-varying covariates |

A subject exits when `in_state == 0` on their last row (`alive = 1` for
discharge, `alive = 0` for death). Subjects still in the active state at
`tmax` have `in_state == 1` on their last row.

### Simulated example data

`sim_bin()` generates an ICU panel with binary treatment and competing exit
events (death vs discharge). The same DGP is used in the package accuracy tests.

```{r sim-panel}
df <- sim_bin(n = 2000L, tmax = 5L, seed = 1L)
head(df)
```

---

## Step 1 — Define a policy

A policy is a function `(D_block, t, a_names)` that returns a `data.table`
with the shifted treatment values for all subjects at time `t`. Here we use a
threshold rule: treat everyone with biomarker `L1 > 1.0` (mandate bundle if
not already on it).

```{r policy}
policy_bin <- function(D_block, t, a_names) {
  out <- D_block[, ..a_names, drop = FALSE]
  out[[a_names[1]]] <- pmax(D_block[[a_names[1]]],
                             as.integer(D_block[["L1"]] > 1.0))
  out
}
```

---

## Step 2 — Density ratios

`fit_g()` fits per-time-point treatment models and returns the
instantaneous ratio $r_t = d\tilde{P}(A_t \mid H_t) / dP(A_t \mid H_t)$
comparing the MTP to the natural course.  The default `method = "classification"`
stacks natural and shifted rows and recovers the ratio as classifier odds; use
`method = "propensity"` for a single binary (0/1) or ordered-factor treatment
when you prefer a direct propensity-score formulation.

```{r density-ratio}
# For real analyses replace with a richer library:
# e.g. c("SL.glm", "SL.earth", "SL.xgboost", "SL.dbarts")
sl_lib <- c("SL.mean", "SL.glm")

wr <- fit_g(
  df              = df,
  a_names         = "A",
  tmax            = 5L,
  baseline        = c("age", "sex"),
  tv_names        = c("L1", "L2"),
  sl_g            = sl_lib,
  k               = 1L,
  inner_v         = 5L,
  v               = 5L,
  seed            = 1L,
  id              = "id",
  time            = "time",
  policy_spec_fun = policy_bin
)
```

`wr$weights_dt` contains one row per subject per time with `Rt_t`
(instantaneous ratio) and `global_fold` (cross-fitting fold). Inspect
`wr$sl_summary` to check SuperLearner ensemble weights.

**Bypass for identical natural and shifted treatment.** At any time point
where the policy produces no shift for any subject (natural treatment =
shifted treatment in every row), `fit_g()` skips model fitting
entirely and fills $r_t = 1$ for all subjects at that time. This covers
policies with a finite intervention window: time points outside the window
are filled with 1 automatically.

### Weights, intervention windows, and trim

**Intervention window shorter than `tmax`.** A common pattern is an MTP
that intervenes only during times 1 to $x < \texttt{tmax}$ (e.g. treatment
is feasible only in the first few ICU days). `fit_g()` is called
with this `tmax`, fits models only where the shift is non-trivial, and fills
$r_t = 1$ outside the intervention window. The downstream estimators
`sdr()` and `itmle()` are still called with the full `tmax`:

- The Q-models covering time points beyond $x$ are estimated under the
  natural course (weights = 1), but the risk set (who is still in the ICU)
  continues to evolve and is modelled correctly. For SDR this means the
  backward recursion propagates through those time points using natural-course
  predictions; for iTMLE the targeting step uses unit weights there.
- Modelling beyond the intervention window is therefore still useful: it
  correctly accounts for transitions that occur after the policy has ended.

**Trimming.** Trim is applied **globally** across the entire `weights_dt`
object at the point it is consumed by `sdr()` or `itmle()`. The trim quantile
is computed over all time points present in the weight object, not just those
within the intervention window or the current `tmax`. This means:

- The trim threshold is identical regardless of whether you call the
  estimator with `tmax = 3` or `tmax = 10`, as long as they share the same
  weight object — estimates across horizons are directly comparable.
- The same `trim` value must be passed consistently to all estimators that
  share a weight object.

### Using `dr_sl = TRUE` (Wu-Benkeser metalearner)

By default (`dr_sl = FALSE`) treatment models are binary classifiers and the
density ratio is recovered as $\hat{r} = \hat{p} / (1 - \hat{p})$. Setting
`dr_sl = TRUE` switches to the Wu-Benkeser (2024) metalearner, which
minimises a density-ratio loss directly on the simplex.

**This requires custom SuperLearner wrappers that return density ratios
directly, not class probabilities.** The package does not export such wrappers
because the right design choices (learner type, regularisation, bandwidth) are
analysis-specific. The `fit_g()` help page documents the interface a
custom wrapper must satisfy.

---

## Step 3 — SDR estimator

```{r sdr}
res_sdr <- sdr(
  df              = df,
  weight_object   = wr,
  tmax            = 5L,
  id              = "id",
  time            = "time",
  alive           = "alive",
  in_state        = "in_state",
  y               = "Y",
  baseline        = c("age", "sex"),
  tv_names        = c("L1", "L2"),
  a_names         = "A",
  sl_remain       = sl_lib,
  sl_death        = sl_lib,
  sl_recursive    = sl_lib,
  sl_y            = sl_lib,
  outcome_family  = "binomial",
  k               = 1L,
  inner_v         = 5L,
  seed            = 1L,
  policy_spec_fun = policy_bin
)

cat(sprintf(
  "SDR  psi = %.3f  (natural = %.3f)  SE = %.3f  95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
  res_sdr$psi, res_sdr$decomposition$psi_plugin_nat, res_sdr$se,
  res_sdr$ci[1], res_sdr$ci[2]
))
```

The return list contains `psi` (point estimate under MTP), `se` (from the
efficient influence curve), `ci`, `ic_df` (per-subject IC values),
`predictions` (`$natural`, `$shifted` Q-matrix), `decomposition`
(`$psi_plugin_nat`, `$psi_plugin_shf`), and `diagnostics`.

---

## Step 4 — Infinite-dimensional TMLE (iTMLE)

iTMLE applies an infinite-dimensional TMLE fluctuation as the update step.
It requires `sl_tmle`: a SuperLearner library of targeting wrappers from the
`sl_itmle` family that handle the logit offset passed as column `._sl_offset`
in the design matrix. These are the **only** SL wrappers the package exports,
because they must accommodate the offset-as-column structure that standard
SuperLearner wrappers do not handle (see `?sl_itmle`).

For a quick start, `SL.tgt.intercept` (standard one-parameter TMLE update)
and `SL.tgt.glm` (GLM fluctuation) are sufficient. The full `sl_tmle` default
vector adds penalised regression and gradient boosting.

```{r itmle}
res_itmle <- itmle(
  df               = df,
  weight_object    = wr,
  tmax             = 5L,
  id               = "id",
  time             = "time",
  alive            = "alive",
  in_state         = "in_state",
  y                = "Y",
  baseline         = c("age", "sex"),
  tv_names         = c("L1", "L2"),
  a_names          = "A",
  sl_remain        = sl_lib,
  sl_death         = sl_lib,
  sl_recursive     = sl_lib,
  sl_y             = sl_lib,
  sl_tmle          = c("SL.tgt.intercept", "SL.tgt.glm"),
  outcome_family   = "binomial",
  k                = 1L,
  inner_v          = 5L,
  v_target_itmle   = 5L,
  v_sl_inner_itmle = 5L,
  seed             = 1L,
  policy_spec_fun  = policy_up
)

cat(sprintf(
  "iTMLE  psi = %.3f  SE = %.3f  95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]\n",
  res_itmle$psi, res_itmle$se,
  res_itmle$ci[1], res_itmle$ci[2]
))
```

`diagnostics$target_cal` tracks the mean EIF and fluctuation parameter per
targeting iteration; values near zero confirm the targeting step converged.

---

## Step 5 — Q-recursion sensitivity check (`qreg`)

`qreg()` runs the same backward Q-regression without any update step. The
point estimate $\hat\Psi_Q = n^{-1}\sum_i \hat{Q}_1(H_{i1})$ depends only on
the Q-models and is independent of density-ratio weights.

It is **not** sequentially doubly robust and carries first-order bias when
Q-models are misspecified. Use it as a sensitivity check: if `qreg` and `sdr`
agree, the DR update and density-ratio weighting are not decisive. A large
discrepancy suggests extreme weights or Q-model misspecification and warrants
closer inspection of ESS diagnostics.

Passing `weight_object` is optional but enables an EIF-based SE alongside the
always-computed naive SE (which treats the fitted Q as fixed and
underestimates uncertainty).

```{r qreg}
res_qreg <- qreg(
  df              = df,
  tmax            = 5L,
  id              = "id",
  time            = "time",
  alive           = "alive",
  in_state        = "in_state",
  y               = "Y",
  baseline        = c("age", "sex"),
  tv_names        = c("L1", "L2"),
  a_names         = "A",
  sl_remain       = sl_lib,
  sl_death        = sl_lib,
  sl_recursive    = sl_lib,
  sl_y            = sl_lib,
  outcome_family  = "binomial",
  k               = 1L,
  inner_v         = 5L,
  seed            = 1L,
  policy_spec_fun = policy_bin
)

cat(sprintf(
  "qreg  estimate = %.3f  SE (naive) = %.3f\n",
  res_qreg$psi, res_qreg$decomposition$se_naive
))
```

---

## Diagnostics

All estimators return diagnostic objects alongside the point estimate.

### SuperLearner weights — `diagnostics$sl_summary`

A `data.table` of ensemble weights per fold, time point, and model component
(`g_remain`, `g_death_exit`, `Q_exit`, `Q_rem`). Check that no single learner
dominates unexpectedly and that weights are stable across folds.

```{r sl-summary}
head(res_sdr$diagnostics$sl_summary)
```

### Per-fold summaries — `diagnostics$recursion_diag`

Counts and mean Q predictions per fold and time point. Useful for spotting
time points with very few at-risk subjects, which can destabilise model fits.

```{r fold-diag}
res_sdr$diagnostics$recursion_diag
```

### Branch calibration — `diagnostics$branch_cal` (SDR / qreg)

Compares in-fold training vs. held-out validation performance (AUC, Brier
score, MSE) for each model component at each time point. A large
training–validation gap signals overfitting.

```{r branch-cal}
head(res_sdr$diagnostics$branch_cal)
```

### Targeting diagnostics — `diagnostics$target_cal` (iTMLE only)

Tracks the mean EIF and the fluctuation parameter $\epsilon$ across targeting
iterations. Values near zero confirm the targeting step has solved the
efficient score equation.

```{r target-diag}
head(res_itmle$diagnostics$target_cal)
```

### Density-ratio ESS

`wr$weights_dt` provides `Rt_t` (instantaneous ratio) and `cum_ratio`
(cumulative product) per subject per time. Monitor the effective sample size
(ESS) of the cumulative weights — ESS collapse across time is the main
practical failure mode of density-ratio-based estimators and will inflate
standard errors even when the point estimate looks stable.

---

## Exit states and absorption

Patients leave the active state at every time point — in ICU cohorts typically
50–80% before the treatment window ends. Treating exit as censoring targets a
counterfactual world without discharge and cannot form composite outcomes that
combine death and discharge. `CausalState` treats each exit as a branch in the
backward recursion; `absorb_rule()` fixes the outcome in branches where it is
known rather than estimating it with `sl_y`.

This is the feature that distinguishes `CausalState` from `lmtp`: exit
outcomes can be deterministic (known at exit time) or stochastic (modelled),
per branch and per use case.

### Mortality (binary outcome)

In-ICU death fixes the outcome to 1. Discharge is stochastic — patients may
die post-discharge — so the discharge branch is modelled by `sl_y`.

```{r absorb-mort}
df_mort <- sim_bin(n = 2000L, tmax = 5L, seed = 1L, outcome = "mort")

res_mort <- sdr(
  df              = df_mort,
  weight_object   = wr,       # fit_g() run with the same df
  tmax            = 5L,
  id = "id", time = "time", alive = "alive", in_state = "in_state",
  y               = "Y",
  baseline        = c("age", "sex"),
  tv_names        = c("L1", "L2"),
  a_names         = "A",
  sl_remain       = sl_lib, sl_death = sl_lib,
  sl_recursive    = sl_lib, sl_y    = sl_lib,
  outcome_family  = "binomial",
  k = 1L, inner_v = 5L, seed = 1L,
  policy_spec_fun = policy_bin,
  absorb          = list(
    absorb_rule(alive == 0, value = 1, branch = "death")
  )
)
```

### Days alive and out of hospital to day 30 (DAOH-30)

In-ICU death gives 0 days. Discharge is stochastic (post-discharge death
or prolonged ward stay reduce days). Use `outcome_family = "gaussian"` and
`y_bounds = c(0, 30)` so the internal `[0,1]` scaling uses the correct range.

```{r absorb-daoh}
df_daoh <- sim_bin(n = 2000L, tmax = 5L, seed = 1L, outcome = "daoh")

res_daoh <- sdr(
  df              = df_daoh,
  weight_object   = wr,
  tmax            = 5L,
  id = "id", time = "time", alive = "alive", in_state = "in_state",
  y               = "Y",
  baseline        = c("age", "sex"),
  tv_names        = c("L1", "L2"),
  a_names         = "A",
  sl_remain       = sl_lib, sl_death = sl_lib,
  sl_recursive    = sl_lib, sl_y    = sl_lib,
  outcome_family  = "gaussian",
  y_bounds        = c(0, 30),
  k = 1L, inner_v = 5L, seed = 1L,
  policy_spec_fun = policy_bin,
  absorb          = list(
    absorb_rule(alive == 0, value = 0, branch = "death")
  )
)
```

### ICU-free days (deterministic discharge branch)

If post-discharge outcomes are excluded by design, the discharge outcome is
known exactly: `30 - t` days. Both branches can be absorbed, leaving `sl_y`
unused.

```{r absorb-icufd}
res_icufd <- sdr(
  ...,
  y_bounds        = c(0, 30),
  outcome_family  = "gaussian",
  absorb          = list(
    absorb_rule(alive == 0,    value = 0,      branch = "death"),
    absorb_rule(in_state == 0, value = 30 - t, branch = "dc")
  )
)
```

For the penalised definition where post-discharge death counts as 0 days,
remove the `"dc"` rule and let `sl_y` model the discharge branch.

---

## Categorical (ordinal) treatment

Categorical treatments must be supplied as **factors**. Use an **ordered
factor** for ordinal treatment, declaring its level order explicitly.
There is no separate `treatment_levels` argument.

`sim_cat()` returns a panel with an ordered four-level treatment:
0 = none, 1 = low, 2 = medium, 3 = high.

```{r sim-cat}
df_cat <- sim_cat(n = 2000L, tmax = 5L, seed = 1L)
levels(df_cat$A)
is.ordered(df_cat$A)
```

For your own data, declare the treatment before fitting:

```{r factor-treatment, eval=FALSE}
patient_data$A <- factor(patient_data$A, levels = 0:3, ordered = TRUE)
# Named categories work as well:
patient_data$A <- factor(
  patient_data$A, levels = c("none", "low", "medium", "high"), ordered = TRUE
)
```

Numeric columns retain numeric coding; CausalState does not guess whether
an integer-valued treatment is categorical. Use ordinary factors for
unordered categories with classification density-ratio estimation.

Policies receive the factor column itself. The following policy escalates
patients with high acuity (`L1 > 0.5`) to at least the third dose level.
The category indices are used only to implement the declared order;
returned values use the original category labels:

```{r policy-cat}
policy_cat <- function(D_block, t, a_names) {
  out <- D_block[, ..a_names, drop = FALSE]
  a <- D_block[[a_names[1]]]
  rank <- as.integer(a)
  eligible <- D_block[["L1"]] > 0.5
  rank[eligible] <- pmax(rank[eligible], 3L)
  out[[a_names[1]]] <- factor(
    levels(a)[rank], levels = levels(a), ordered = is.ordered(a)
  )
  out
}
```

A policy can also return category labels, for example `list(A = "2")`
for a fixed assignment to the level labelled `"2"`. CausalState restores
the input factor's complete level set and ordered status. Unknown
categories are rejected. Numeric outputs for a factor are matched to
the actual category labels; they are never treated as internal factor codes.

Use `method = "propensity"` for direct ordinal propensity estimation:

```{r fit-g-cat}
wr_cat <- fit_g(
  df = df_cat, a_names = "A", tmax = 5L,
  baseline = "age", tv_names = "L1",
  sl_g = sl_lib, method = "propensity",
  k = 1L, inner_v = 5L, v = 5L, seed = 1L,
  id = "id", time = "time", policy_spec_fun = policy_cat
)
```

The treatment model fits binomial SuperLearners for
\(P(A > a_j \mid A \ge a_j,H)\), using the declared factor order.
These continuation probabilities give a coherent probability for each dose
without a proportional-odds assumption.

The policy distribution sums all source categories that map to a
destination:
\(g^*(a\mid h) = \sum_b I\{d(b,h)=a\}g(b\mid h)\).
For an eligible patient, the minimum-dose rule gives dose 2 probability
`g(0|H) + g(1|H) + g(2|H)`; doses 0 and 1 have zero policy probability.
Many-to-one rules work directly, with no inverse policy required.

Ordinal propensity supports one ordered factor and deterministic
category assignments. The policy must depend on current treatment and
pre-treatment history and must also work at hypothetical category values.
Each declared category needs training observations in every outer fold;
upper-dose risk sets must meet the learners' sample-size and event
requirements. Numeric binary 0/1 propensity keeps its existing stochastic
policy interface.

To compare methods, refit the same factor data with
`method = "classification"`. Neither method is uniformly preferable:
classification models the policy ratio directly; ordinal propensity
models the category distribution and applies the policy mapping exactly.

Every learner receives the same numeric reference indicators for factor
treatments: three columns for four levels, with the first level as
reference. The same coding applies to current and lagged treatment,
transition and Q models, and iTMLE targeting history. Policy application
rebuilds current-category indicators and preserves observed history.
Unused factor levels retain their indicator columns in fitting subsets.

This permits separate category effects in GLMs without requiring equal
increments per dose unit. It does not impose a monotone response or
automatically add treatment-history interactions. Custom wrappers receive
already encoded treatment predictors; other categorical covariates remain
the wrappers' responsibility.

Factor levels and ordered status are recorded in
`wr_cat$settings$treatment_levels` and `wr_cat$settings$treatment_ordered`.
Pass the complete `wr_cat` object to `sdr()` or `itmle()`, together with
the same factor data, to check this schema automatically. `qreg()` infers
its coding directly from its input factors. No downstream levels argument
is needed, including when passing only a weights table.

For multiple treatments with classification, make each categorical
treatment a factor and leave continuous treatments numeric.

```{r sdr-cat}
res_sdr_cat <- sdr(
  df = df_cat, weight_object = wr_cat, tmax = 5L,
  id = "id", time = "time", alive = "alive", in_state = "in_state", y = "Y",
  baseline = "age", tv_names = "L1", a_names = "A",
  sl_remain = sl_lib, sl_death = sl_lib,
  sl_recursive = sl_lib, sl_y = sl_lib,
  outcome_family = "binomial", k = 1L, inner_v = 5L,
  parallel = FALSE, seed = 1L, policy_spec_fun = policy_cat
)
res_sdr_cat$psi
res_sdr_cat$se
```

## Parallelism

All estimators default to `parallel = FALSE` and `parallel_t = FALSE` and run
on a single core out of the box.

**Two independent levels of parallelism are available**, both implemented via
`parallel::mclapply()` (process forking):

1. **Fold-level** (`parallel = TRUE`, `fold_workers`): each cross-fitting
   fold runs in a separate forked process.
2. **Within-fold regression** (`reg_workers`): per-time-point regression
   tasks within each fold are distributed across worker processes.
3. **Time-point level in `fit_g()`** (`parallel_t = TRUE`,
   `t_workers`): time points are parallelised independently of fold workers.

Because forking is used, **this does not work on Windows**. On Linux and
macOS, set BLAS, xgboost, and dbarts thread counts to 1 before enabling
process-level parallelism to avoid oversubscription:

```{r parallel}
# Example: 5-fold outer parallelism on Linux/macOS
res_sdr_par <- sdr(
  ...,
  parallel     = TRUE,
  fold_workers = 5L,
  reg_workers  = 1L      # keep inner regressions single-threaded
)
```
